stories.headline: TREASURY SECRETARY BESSENT SAYS A HORMUZ DEAL COULD COME 'TODAY OR TOMORROW,' SENDING STOCKS TO RECORD HIGHS AS OIL WHIPSAWS
stories.body: Scott Bessent said Tuesday 'we are in talks with the Iranians' and there is a chance of a deal 'to open the Strait and move towards a more normalized position' within a day, while Trump called his own proposal Tehran's 'final opportunity'; equities read the comments as bullish even as Iran maintained it has no direct talks underway, only indirect discussions via Oman.
stories.explain: Markets are trading the probability of a durable Hormuz reopening, not the underlying diplomatic ambiguity, which is why stocks rallied on a Treasury Secretary's optimism that Iran's own foreign ministry didn't confirm. A reopened Strait permanently removes the tail-risk premium built into oil, credit, and equity vol simultaneously, so even a partial move toward that outcome gets priced across every asset class at once. The gap between Bessent's 'today or tomorrow' framing and Iran's 'indirect talks only' stance is exactly the kind of headline risk that can reverse Tuesday's gains in a single session if the two sides' accounts diverge further.

stories.headline: S&P 500 AND DOW CLOSE AT RECORD HIGHS, NASDAQ 100 SURGES 3.27% AS CHIP STOCKS AND AMAZON, PALANTIR EARNINGS FUEL A TECH COMEBACK
stories.body: The S&P 500 jumped 1.79% to a record 7,736.52 and the Dow added 907 points (1.71%) to 54,085.88, while the Nasdaq 100 led with a 3.27% surge as semiconductor names rebounded and strong prints from Amazon and Palantir reignited the AI trade; the broader Nasdaq Composite gained 2.59% to 26,584.99.
stories.explain: The Nasdaq 100's outsized 3.27% move against the S&P's 1.79% is a concentration effect: the index is cap-weighted toward a handful of mega-cap tech and chip names, so when those specific stocks beat earnings and rally together, the index can swing multiples harder than a more diversified benchmark on the same news. Falling yields amplify this mechanically too, since tech and chip valuations lean on long-duration cash flow forecasts that get discounted more heavily when rates are higher, so today's drop in the 10-year yield lowered the discount rate right as earnings beat expectations. That combination, a lower discount rate plus higher expected cash flows, is why growth-heavy indices outperform value-heavy ones on days like this.

stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD EASES TO 4.64% EVEN AS FED FUNDS FUTURES PRICE A 68% CHANCE OF A SEPTEMBER RATE HIKE
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield slipped roughly 4 basis points to 4.64% Tuesday as falling oil eased near-term inflation expectations, even though fed funds futures are now pricing about a 68% probability of a 25-basis-point hike at the September FOMC meeting after three officials dissented from last week's hold in favor of tightening sooner.
stories.explain: Fed funds futures translate directly into a hike probability because the contract price is just 100 minus the market's expected average fed funds rate for that contract month; comparing the September contract's implied rate to the current target gives the roughly 68% odds being quoted. The 10-year yield can still fall even as those near-term hike odds rise because long-term yields price the average expected rate path years out plus a term premium, not just the next meeting, and today's oil-driven drop in expected future inflation outweighs the modestly higher near-term rate path. That's the mechanism behind a flattening move: short rates anchored or rising on hike odds, long rates falling on improving inflation expectations, compressing the spread between them.

stories.headline: WTI CRUDE REBOUNDS 3% TO $81.80, CLAWING BACK PART OF MONDAY'S PLUNGE AS HORMUZ TALKS REMAIN UNCONFIRMED
stories.body: West Texas Intermediate rose roughly 3% to $81.80 a barrel and Brent pushed toward $85 as traders partially reversed Monday's 6.2% war-risk-premium unwind, with the bounce reflecting genuine uncertainty over whether Bessent's optimistic Hormuz timeline will actually be confirmed by Tehran.
stories.explain: This is the same risk-premium mechanism running in reverse from Monday: no barrels changed hands differently in the Strait today, so the 3% bounce is the market re-adding some probability-weighted disruption risk it had just priced out, not a reaction to a real supply shift. A premium that swings 6% down and 3% up across two sessions on rhetoric alone, rather than tanker data or OPEC output changes, tells you the market currently has almost no conviction in either direction and is trading headlines rather than fundamentals. That instability is itself useful information for an inflation forecast: a premium this volatile is unlikely to show up as a persistent input to core CPI, since a durable deal would collapse it and a real supply shock would move it far more than 6%.

stories.headline: AMAZON TOPS $3 TRILLION MARKET CAP BUT SLIDES 2% AS BEZOS FILES TO SELL $4 BILLION IN SHARES; SPACEX REVENUE NEARLY DOUBLES TO $7.8B DESPITE A $541M LOSS
stories.body: Amazon crossed a $3 trillion market cap for the first time Tuesday even as its shares fell about 2% after Jeff Bezos filed to sell roughly $4 billion of stock, while SpaceX reported revenue nearly doubling to $7.8 billion (above forecasts) alongside a $541 million net loss, with the stock closing at $125.33, down sharply from its post-IPO peak of $225.64 after June's $75 billion capital raise.
stories.explain: Bezos's sale filing and Amazon's stock dip on the same day it hit a valuation milestone illustrates a basic supply-and-demand mechanic in equity markets: a large pending share sale from a known insider signals additional supply hitting the float, and traders price that in ahead of the actual transaction regardless of the company's underlying momentum. SpaceX's outcome, a near-doubling of revenue paired with a still-wide net loss and a stock more than 40% off its IPO peak, is a reminder that growth-stage private-to-public companies are often valued on a multiple of expected future cash flows rather than current profitability, so any signal that the growth trajectory is uncertain compresses the multiple even when the top-line beats estimates.

stories.headline: SENATE'S PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT GAINS BIG TEN, SEC BACKING AS COURT-ORDERED FIFTH-YEAR TRANSFER WINDOW ENTERS ITS SECOND DAY
stories.body: The Senate is working through procedural steps on an updated draft of the Protect College Sports Act that won endorsement from the Big Ten and SEC, while NCAA president Charlie Baker continues urging Congress to pass it; separately, the special transfer portal window opened under Judge Charlotte Sweeney's fifth-year-eligibility injunction runs through Aug. 10, and Michigan State point guard Jeremy Fears withdrew from the NBA draft to return to the Spartans.

stories.headline: LEBRON JAMES STILL UNSIGNED AS WARRIORS TURN COOL ON PURSUIT; AGENT RICH PAUL MAPS OUT REMAINING DESTINATIONS
stories.body: LeBron James remains the biggest name on the free-agent market with training camps a month away, as ESPN reports the Warriors are now pessimistic about landing him and agent Rich Paul is working through a shortlist of alternative destinations; elsewhere, Dallas signed Naji Marshall to a three-year, $51.86 million extension and Portland inked Jeremy Sochan for one year at $2.63 million.

stories.headline: BIJAN ROBINSON BECOMES HIGHEST-PAID RUNNING BACK IN NFL HISTORY ON THREE-YEAR, UP-TO-$75 MILLION FALCONS EXTENSION
stories.body: Atlanta signed Bijan Robinson to a three-year extension worth up to $75 million, making him the league's highest-paid running back, on the same day Baltimore locked up receiver Zay Flowers on a four-year, $140 million deal; both moves came as training camps around the league logged a fresh round of injuries, including Eagles receivers Makai Lemon and DeVonta Smith sitting out Tuesday's practice with hamstring issues.

stories.headline: ALABAMA'S QB COMPETITION TIGHTENS BETWEEN KEELON RUSSELL AND AUSTIN MACK AS FALL CAMP OPENS ACROSS THE COUNTRY
stories.body: Alabama head coach Kalen DeBoer said Austin Mack may hold a slight edge in the Crimson Tide's starting quarterback battle with Keelon Russell due to his familiarity with the offense, though Russell's athleticism keeps the race open with both expected to see the field in the opener; fall camp storylines elsewhere include Bill Belichick's four-man quarterback competition at North Carolina and Mario Cristobal finalizing a long-term extension at Miami.

sports.detail: UW unveiled its 2026 game-day themes; season opens Sept. 6 vs. Washington State (Apple Cup) at Husky Stadium under third-year coach Jedd Fisch. Jordan Washington likely out for the year after a spring head/neck injury.

UW landed Rutgers transfer Harun Zrno (6-7 guard), filling the roster to 15 for Danny Sprinkle's third season. The Huskies lost leading scorers Hannes Steinbach and Zoom Diallo and added ex-NBA assistant Charles Klask to the staff.

Seahawks held a non-padded practice Tuesday with a new injury concern around fullback Robbie Ouzts. HBO's 'Hard Knocks,' featuring the defending Super Bowl champions, premieres tonight at 9 p.m. ET/PT.

Center Jalen Duren's contract standoff with Detroit remains unresolved, with talks reportedly stretching deep into August; the Pistons are coming off a 60-win season and enter a reshaped East as LeBron James' free agency plays out.
Mariners (55-58) host the Tigers (54-58) at T-Mobile Park in the series opener tonight. Seattle is 32-24 at home this season.

deepDive.title: How Fed Funds Futures Price a Rate Hike — and Why Long Yields Can Still Fall
content: Today's brief has a puzzle in it: fed funds futures are pricing roughly a 68% chance the Fed hikes in September, yet the 10-year Treasury yield eased to 4.64%, down about 4 basis points on the day. If the market thinks a hike is more likely than not, why would the yield on a much longer bond be falling instead of rising? The answer is that the two numbers are measuring different things, and understanding the gap between them is one of the more useful mechanical lessons in fixed income for anyone trying to read a day like today correctly.

Fed funds futures are contracts that settle based on the average effective fed funds rate over a given month, and their price is quoted as 100 minus that expected rate. If the September contract implies an average rate noticeably above today's target, you can back out an implied probability of a hike by comparing that gap to the size of a standard 25-basis-point move; that's the arithmetic behind the 'CME FedWatch'-style probabilities you see quoted, and it's why the 68% figure moved today after Friday's hawkish dissents. Crucially, this only reflects the market's read on the next one or two meetings, not the rate path five or ten years out.

The 10-year yield, by contrast, is roughly the average expected path of short-term rates over the next decade plus a term premium investors demand for locking up money that long. A single meeting's hike odds barely move that average, while a shift in long-run inflation expectations moves it a lot. Today's oil bounce aside, the broader signal since Monday has been that a Hormuz resolution would remove a persistent inflation risk that had been keeping long-run expectations elevated, and that repricing lowers the whole curve's average expected path even as near-term hike odds tick up. The 1994 hiking cycle is the classic historical case of this decoupling, when short rates rose sharply on Fed action while the long end moved far less, because the market believed the Fed would tame inflation rather than let it compound.

For a portfolio, the practical read is that today's move is a flattening signal, not a dovish one: short rates anchored or drifting higher on hike odds, long rates drifting lower on improving inflation expectations, which compresses the 10-year to fed-funds spread. Watch Thursday's CPI print closely, since a hot number would raise both the hike probability and long-run inflation expectations together, steepening things back out, while a soft number would do the opposite and likely pull the hike odds down with it. The two numbers moving in opposite directions today isn't a contradiction; it's the yield curve doing exactly what it's supposed to do when a near-term policy signal and a long-run inflation signal diverge.
